through_line: The harness matters more than the model. Airbnb, Meta and Google all report that their gains came from what they built around the agent: shared context through tool servers, ways for the agent to check its own work, and pass/fail evals that block a bad merge. Today's Learn read makes the same move for permissions: Figma got control back by turning rules into data that can be checked.

items.title: How Figma pulled permissions out of one giant if/else
items.summary: Day two: how a permission check actually runs. Figma's single has_access? function had grown boolean flags nobody dared touch and was about 20% of database load, so they split every rule into small allow/deny policies (deny always wins) written as JSON, kept data loading separate, and evaluated lazily so a check stops as soon as one policy decides. Their debugger and null-comparison linter show what you get once rules are data rather than code. The second read is the short version of the golden rule: check permissions, never role names.

also.title: Contentsquare: check permissions, not roles, and keep grants additive (2018)

items.title: Airbnb wired its internal tools into one coding agent
items.summary: Airbnb's CTO on how 60% of their code came to be AI-authored: one internal agent that carries company context through MCP servers, a context graph of past projects that cut a six-to-nine-month build to about six weeks for the next similar one, and async agents that wake on monitoring alerts to do first-pass on-call triage. It also covers picking a different model per job: the strongest one for coding, small post-trained ones for latency-sensitive search.

items.title: Google binds OAuth refresh tokens to a key, not a bearer
items.summary: A stolen bearer token works for whoever holds it. DPoP ties the token to a private key on the client, so a copy is useless without the key. The interesting part is the trade-off: Google binds only the long-lived refresh token, because checking a signature on every access-token call would cost too much CPU at their request rates. It also explains why one agent can't sign for another when tasks get handed down a chain.

items.title: Anthropic gives outside evaluators employee-level access
items.summary: A team from METR now gets company laptops, internal tools and the right to publish without a veto. The post sets out three tiers of evaluator access and compares the setup to bank examiners who work inside the banks they supervise. It's a short look at how outside auditing of AI models is being set up, and where it stops: architecture and customer data stay off-limits.

items.title: Stanford generates text coarse-to-fine, not token by token
items.summary: Instead of predicting one token after another, NCM compresses text into a few levels of codes, rough gist first and detail last, and fills in each level in one parallel step. A step-through of a German-to-English translation shows rough drafts sharpening level by level. At around 100M parameters it runs 10-31x faster than strong diffusion language models at similar quality and solves the most hard Sudokus. It's still early and small-scale.

items.title: Meta built a whole app with the engineer supervising the loop
items.summary: The Forum team let agents plan, build and test their own work, while engineers set goals and signed off. A task only counted as done once tests and visual checks passed. Their biggest gains came from giving the agent tools to inspect the live app instead of describing it, which sharply cut edits to the wrong screen. A stress-testing loop caught a memory problem before launch, and fixing it roughly halved memory use.

items.title: Testing agents properly: read 20 traces first, judge yes/no
items.summary: A practical playbook for testing agents. Start by reading 20 traces by hand and marking every wrong tool call or loop. Turn those notes into pass/fail checks, because LLM judges can't hold a 1-to-5 scale steady. Count latency, tokens and tool calls alongside answer quality. Then block merges when any check that used to pass fails. Expect 50-60 small tweaks to reach production quality, not one big rewrite.

items.title: Meta's GPU network: eight planes per GPU, cable length matters
items.summary: Skip the hardware launches and read the fabric sections. Each GPU now connects to eight separate network planes, and the network card spreads every packet across all of them, which removes a whole tier of switches. When one cluster stretches across buildings, lossless Ethernet needs buffer space in proportion to cable length, so the switches measure their own cables with timed probes and size the buffers to match.

items.title: The AWS DNS outage race, rebuilt as a TLA+ model
items.summary: Murat Demirbas models the race behind the October 2025 DynamoDB outage. The model only found the bug once one atomic step was split into three: receive a plan, apply it, clean up old plans. With that split, a slow worker applies a stale plan that the cleanup then deletes. It's a short worked example of how breaking up a step exposes a check-then-act race, and you can step through the failing trace in your browser.
